name: Bloom
summary: The whitish, powdery wax coating naturally found on blueberries (and some other fruit) that protects the fruit and affects its visual appearance.
what_is_it: Bloom is a natural, whitish, powdery epicuticular wax layer that forms on the skin of blueberries and several other fruits as they ripen. It is not dirt, residue, or a defect -- it is a fruit-produced coating.
why_it_matters: Bloom acts as a natural barrier that helps reduce moisture loss and can offer some protection against decay-causing organisms, contributing to postharvest quality. It is also a visual cue: a heavy, even bloom is often associated by consumers and buyers with fresher, less-handled fruit, since bloom can rub off with repeated handling.
how_evaluated: Bloom is assessed visually and by handling -- how even and heavy the wax coating appears, and how well it survives packing and transport. There is no standard instrument measurement in general commercial use; it is typically described qualitatively (heavy, light, patchy, rubbed) in trial notes or marketing material.
what_affects_it: Genetics determines how much wax a variety naturally produces. Handling intensity during harvest and packing, moisture, and physical contact during transport can visibly reduce bloom even though the underlying fruit quality is unaffected.
how_to_interpret: Bloom is a visual/handling characteristic, not a food-safety or ripeness indicator by itself -- reduced bloom from normal handling does not necessarily mean lower fruit quality. Where bloom is mentioned in a variety or commercial claim, note whether it is describing a genetic trait of the variety or the observed condition of a specific shipment.
